Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

Do not perform the task.", "input": "i need a clear prompt for writing the volunteer packet for the new board-game lending shelf, not the packet itself yet. it’s called Roll Call and it’s in the Maple Room at Harborlight Neighborhood House, 18 Alder Lane. the first public day is october 3. make the packet sound welcoming and practical, like it’s for neighbors who might not know the volunteers or the rules yet, and for volunteers who need to know what to do without having to guess. We’re not a shop and this isn’t a paid membership thing. Please use the name Roll Call consistently; Harborlight Neighborhood House is the place, not the name of the shelf.

The shelf has 24 boxed games at the start, including two copies of Lantern Market and two of River Routes. The other games are different titles, and there are family games, strategy games, and a few that take less than half an hour. Don’t make up a list of all 24 titles or claim that every game is suitable for every age. A small printed card with each game has its title, suggested player count, approximate playing time, and a component checklist. Volunteers have one paper inventory sheet in the Maple Room, not a computer system. If you mention the inventory, describe that sheet, and don’t imply we already have a reservation website or an online catalogue.

Please make two parts: a public borrowing guide, then an internal volunteer handover for the first month. The guide can explain how a neighbor signs up, borrows a game, and brings it back. Sign-up is a name and a way to contact the borrower; we don’t ask for identification or a fee. One household can borrow up to two games at once for 14 days. They can ask for one renewal if nobody is waiting for that game. No need to promise a renewal before checking for a hold. We’re open for borrowing and returns Wednesdays from 4 to 6 p.m. and Saturdays from 10 a.m. to noon. Don’t say people can drop games off when the Maple Room is unattended; the volunteers need to receive returns during those hours.

The public wording should feel neighborly rather than strict. A parent may come with a child, but the adult is responsible for the borrowed games and the return date. Don’t add a late fee, replacement charge, penalty, or rule about requiring an adult to sign up. The guide can invite people to ask a volunteer for help choosing a game, but shouldn’t promise that a volunteer will teach every game. It might be useful to include this ordinary exchange as an example: a neighbor asks, “Could I borrow both copies of Lantern Market for our club?” and a volunteer says, “You can borrow up to two games, but we keep a copy on the shelf when we can.” Don’t turn that example into a new reservation policy or imply the second copy is always available.

For the internal part, explain who does the regular work. Nora Bell coordinates the volunteers and keeps the paper inventory sheet in the Maple Room. Dev Shah checks returned games and handles simple repairs. Lila Ortiz welcomes new borrowers and records their contact details on the sign-up sheet. The three volunteers share opening and closing shifts; please don’t assign one person every shift or make up extra staff. Nora keeps the room key in the labeled envelope in the front office and signs it out for a shift. A volunteer should return the key to that envelope after closing. Mention that sign-up details stay in the Maple Room folder and are used to contact borrowers about their own loans, not for a public list.

There is one important closing procedure, and I want the two branches kept explicit, not blurred together. At Saturday closing, for each returned game, the volunteer checks its components against the card in the box. If any listed component is missing, do not put that game back on the shelf: put a yellow hold card inside a clear pouch with the game, then move it to the repair crate for Dev. If no listed component is missing, return the game to the shelf after the check. This applies to returned games at Saturday closing, not to games that are still checked out and not to every Wednesday task. A borrower can tell Lila about a missing piece without being accused of losing it; sometimes a piece is found later in a bag or at home. The missing-piece procedure shouldn’t say that a game is automatically retired or that the borrower must pay.

That condition also affects what happens later, so keep the follow-up timing straight. If the missing component is found by Tuesday at noon, Dev puts it with the game and updates the paper inventory sheet, and the game can be checked again before it goes back on the shelf. If the component has not been found by Tuesday at noon, Lila contacts the last borrower privately before the next Saturday opening to ask whether it turned up. Don’t say she contacts them sooner, post their name, or assume the piece is permanently lost. If it turns up after that message, the volunteer who receives it gives it to Dev; don’t have the public guide promise a particular result.

Please include a numbered section called “Saturday closing check” in the internal handover. It should be a usable checklist, with these steps in order: collect returns received by closing; compare each game’s contents with its component card; use the missing-component branch or the complete-game branch above; update the paper inventory sheet with the return and any hold; put the key back in its labeled envelope in the front office. It should not suggest leaving the room open after noon or leaving games unattended. Other practical first-month details: the Maple Room has two folding tables and one low shelf, the component cards are kept inside the game boxes, and the repair crate stays beside the shelf. A volunteer can ask Nora where a form is, but don’t create a new form or invent a phone number.

Use these two ordinary quotes where they fit, without making either one a policy: Nora says, “We’re trying to make it easy to borrow a game and easy to bring it back.” Lila says, “If you’re not sure what’s in the box, we can check the card together.” Keep the distinction between what the public guide tells neighbors and what the internal handover tells volunteers. Please make the final paragraph about the first-month routine, using only these details: Nora reviews the paper inventory sheet with Dev on the first Wednesday after opening, and Lila brings the sign-up sheet to that check so they can see whether the contact details are legible. Don’t add a launch result, approval, recommendation, or a conclusion about how successful the shelf is.", "output": "Write a welcoming, practical volunteer packet for Roll Call, the board-game lending shelf at Harborlight Neighborhood House, 18 Alder Lane. 1. A public borrowing guide explaining sign-up, borrowing, and returns.
2. An internal volunteer handover for the first month.

The shelf starts with 24 boxed games, including two copies each of Lantern Market and River Routes. The remaining games are different titles. - Sign-up requires a name and a way to contact the borrower. No identification or fee is required.

- A child may come with a parent, but the adult is responsible for the borrowed games and return date. Do not add a late fee, replacement charge, penalty, or requirement that an adult sign up.

Keep the public wording neighborly rather than strict. Invite neighbors to ask a volunteer for help choosing a game, without promising that volunteers will teach every game. You may include this exchange as an example, not as a new policy: a neighbor asks, “Could I borrow both copies of Lantern Market for our club?” and a volunteer replies, “You can borrow up to two games, but we keep a copy on the shelf when we can.” Do not imply that the second copy is always available or create a reservation policy.

For the internal handover, describe the existing roles without assigning one person every shift or inventing extra staff. Nora Bell coordinates volunteers and keeps the paper inventory sheet in the Maple Room. Dev Shah checks returned games and handles simple repairs. Lila Ortiz welcomes new borrowers and records their contact details on the sign-up sheet. The three volunteers share opening and closing shifts. Nora keeps the room key in the labeled envelope in the front office and signs it out for a shift; a volunteer returns it to that envelope after closing. Sign-up details stay in the Maple Room folder and are used to contact borrowers about their own loans, not for a public list.

Explain the Saturday closing procedure with both branches clear and separate. At Saturday closing, check each returned game against the component card inside its box. If any listed component is missing, do not return that game to the shelf: put a yellow hold card inside a clear pouch with it, then move it to the repair crate for Dev. If no listed component is missing, return the game to the shelf after the check. This procedure applies to games returned at Saturday closing, not to games still checked out or to every Wednesday task. A borrower may tell Lila about a missing piece without being accused of losing it; pieces are sometimes found later in a bag or at home. Do not say a game is automatically retired or that the borrower must pay.

Keep the later follow-up timing conditional on whether the missing component is found. If it is found by Tuesday at noon, Dev puts it with the game and updates the paper inventory sheet; the game can be checked again before it goes back on the shelf. If it has not been found by Tuesday at noon, Lila contacts the last borrower privately before the next Saturday opening to ask whether it turned up. Do not say she contacts the borrower sooner, post their name, or assume the piece is permanently lost. If the piece turns up after that message, the volunteer who receives it gives it to Dev. Do not promise a particular result in the public guide.

Include this numbered section in the internal handover:

### Saturday closing check
1. Collect returns received by closing.
2. Compare each game’s contents with its component card.
3. Follow the missing-component branch or the complete-game branch above.
4. Update the paper inventory sheet with the return and any hold.
5. Put the key back in its labeled envelope in the front office.

Do not suggest leaving the room open after noon or leaving games unattended. Other first-month details: the Maple Room has two folding tables and one low shelf; component cards are kept inside the game boxes; and the repair crate stays beside the shelf. Volunteers can ask Nora where a form is, but do not create a new form or invent a phone number.

End with a substantive paragraph about the first-month routine, using only these details: on the first Wednesday after opening, Nora reviews the paper inventory sheet with Dev, and Lila brings the sign-up sheet so they can check whether the contact details are legible.
